definition.text: Overfishing is taking fish from a body of water faster than the species can naturally replace itself, so its numbers there keep falling.

facts.text: It can happen in any water body, from ponds and rivers to oceans, and leads to depletion, slower growth and low biomass.
Sustained overfishing can cause critical depensation, where a population can no longer sustain itself and is wiped out locally or globally.
The share of stocks within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 66.9% in 2015.
FAO reported that in 2017, 34 percent of marine fish stocks were overfished.
Collapsed stocks may not return: after trout are overfished, carp can take over and stop trout re-establishing.
Overfishing has reduced fish and marine mammal biomass by 60% since the 1800s.
Illegal catch is estimated at 11 to 26 million tonnes, 14–33% of the world's reported catch.
Remedies include regulation, removing subsidies, gentler fishing gear, aquaculture and consumer awareness.

definition.text: Biologists recognise three types of overfishing: growth overfishing, recruitment overfishing and ecosystem overfishing.

facts.text: Growth overfishing catches fish smaller, on average, than the size that gives the most yield per recruit, so total yield is lower.
Recruitment overfishing depletes the spawning adults until too few remain to replenish the stock.
Recruitment overfishing is treated with moratoriums, quotas and minimum size limits to rebuild spawning biomass.
Ecosystem overfishing shifts the ecosystem toward small forage species as large predators decline.

definition.text: Biological overfishing is fishing so hard that the stock's growth slows; economic overfishing is catching more than the maximum economic yield, where resource rent is highest.

facts.text: Whether there is overfishing depends on what counts as an acceptable level of fishing.
Economic overfishing adds the cost of fishing to the judgement, making the fishery less profitable than it could be.
A dynamic version uses a discount rate to maximise the present value of resource rent over all future catches.

definition.text: A harvest control rule is a set of pre-agreed tools that ties how much may be caught to the estimated state of the stock.

facts.text: Constant catch and constant fishing mortality are two simple types.
Major fisheries worldwide now use harvest control rules with a precautionary approach.
The traffic-light convention sets rules around critical values that are adjusted as more is learned.

definition.text: Fishing capacity is the most a fishery's boats and gear could catch, measured either by the capital fully used (input) or by the maximum catch (output).

facts.text: Output capacity assumes inputs fully used given the stock's biomass and age structure and current technology.
Capacity utilisation compares a fleet's actual catch or inputs with its capacity.
A World Bank and FAO report said half the world's fishing fleet could be scrapped with no change in catch.

definition.text: In an open-access fishery, competition drives fishers to invest until their costs equal their revenue, so the resource rent is wiped out.

facts.text: Because no one can be excluded, a fisher who wants a bigger catch takes it from someone else's share.
Gordon showed that overexploitation and rent dissipation arise in open-access fisheries, rooted in the property rights regime.
Fish move across jurisdictions, so one country's conservation can be exploited by another.
The industry's financial stake leads to lobbying that can block or weaken anti-overfishing policy.
The tragedy of the commons can create perverse incentives for more fisheries subsidies.
